blocks.text: Electron withdrawing groups, such as a halogen atom, have a negative inductive effect (-I). Halogen withdraws bonded electrons from carbon to carbon bond and thus displays negative inductive effect. This causes a permanent dipole to arise in the molecule wherein the halogen atom holds a negative charge and carbon become partial positive Figure 11.12.

blocks.alt: Chain C-C-C-C-Cl with the carbons numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 in red. Red chevrons on the C2-C1 bond (three) and the C1-Cl bond (four) point towards Cl. Charges: delta-delta+ on C2, delta+ on C1, delta- on Cl. Labels: Less positive charge than C1 (arrow onto C2); Less electronegative (C1); More electronegative (Cl); Electron deficient C1 pulling electrons from C1-C2 covalent bond (arrow onto the C2-C1 bond).
blocks.caption: Figure 11.12: Inductive effect: Polarization of sigma bond (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 11.12 marks both C₁ and C₂ ‘δ++’. As the figure’s own label says, C₂ carries a smaller positive charge than C₁: δ⁺ on C₁ and δδ⁺ on C₂, as drawn above.
